answer: A remarkably crowded place I remember was the Eid fair held on an open ground in the centre of our town last year, on the day after Eid-ul-Fitr. After Eid prayers at the mosque and visits to relatives the day before, I went with some old school friends to soak up the atmosphere, and the sheer number of people was staggering. It was so crowded because families from all the surrounding villages come into town for the fair, everyone has a few days off work, and children have new clothes and Eid money to spend. The ground and the streets around it were absolutely packed, with families, vendors and performers filling every inch of space. There were stalls selling toys, bangles and sweets, a small Ferris wheel and even a group of folk singers. At times it was genuinely difficult to move, and the crowd felt almost [[overwhelming]]. Yet despite the crush, there was an [[infectious]] sense of joy in the air that was hard to resist. The whole place was [[buzzing]] with energy, music and the smell of street food. While I would not want to deal with such crowds every day, on that occasion it felt like part of the celebration. I did lose my friends for about twenty minutes, and we only found each other again by shouting. Honestly, being [[swept along]] with so many happy people was strangely [[uplifting]]. It reminded me how such shared events bring an entire community together, even if you do lose a bit of personal space in the process.

followUps.answer: Not really. I find them tiring in everyday situations, such as busy markets or traffic. But at festivals it is different, because everyone shares the same happy mood and the crowd becomes part of the fun.

followUps.q: How do people in your town celebrate Eid?
followUps.answer: The day starts with prayers at the mosque, then people visit relatives, share special food like semai and give money to children. Over the next few days, many families go to fairs or visit friends.

note: An Eid celebration in a 'city centre' became the Eid fair in his own town; added why it was crowded (villagers, holidays, Eid money) and what was there; 'packed' left unmarked, marked 'infectious' and 'swept along'.
